content: Ampicillin, either alone or in combination with gentamicin, is the preferred treatment for listeriosis. For patients who cannot tolerate penicillins, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative option. The recommended duration of therapy varies depending on the clinical presentation. For bacteremia, a minimum of 2 weeks of treatment is advised. Meningitis requires at least 3 weeks of therapy. Endocarditis should be treated for 4 to 6 weeks, while brain abscesses or rhomboencephalitis necessitate a minimum of 6 weeks of treatment. Ampicillin, amoxicillin, and penicillin G are considered effective antibiotics for the treatment of listeriosis. For individuals who are unable to tolerate beta-lactam antibiotics, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole serves as an alternative. Chloramphenicol is not recommended due to its high rates of treatment failure and relapse. The addition of an aminoglycoside, such as gentamicin, is generally advised because it provides synergistic bactericidal effects when combined with ampicillin. This combination is particularly recommended for cases of listerial bacteremia, endocarditis, brain abscess, meningitis, or rhomboencephalitis. For bacteremia, a treatment duration of 2 weeks is sufficient. Meningitis, the most common clinical manifestation of listeriosis, requires antibiotics that achieve good penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and should be treated for at least 3 weeks. Endocarditis necessitates a longer treatment course of 4 to 6 weeks. Brain abscesses or rhomboencephalitis require a minimum of 6 weeks of therapy. Listeria monocytogenes-induced gastroenteritis is typically self-limiting, with complete recovery occurring within approximately 2 days. However, individuals who have consumed food implicated in outbreaks and are at high risk for invasive disease may consider a short course of oral therapy with ampicillin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for several days.
